newsitem.title: USA: Fate of dlr-yen rally eyed as Japan tax hike looms.
newsitem.headline: Fate of dlr-yen rally eyed as Japan tax hike looms.

text.p: The fate of the powerful dollar rally versus the yen could hinge on whether proposed higher taxes in Japan will merely slow that nation's fledgling economic recovery or choke it off, sending the Japanese currency even lower, U.S. experts said.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has vowed to forge ahead with a hike in the sales tax to 5.0 percent from 3.0 percent and to end two trillion yen worth of special income tax cuts when the new fiscal year starts on April 1.
"They are running a tremendous risk by raising taxes in this environment," said Robert McGee, senior economist at Tokai Bank Ltd.
"The last thing you want to do in an economy that hasn't really recovered for seven years from a big deflationary shock is to raise taxes," McGee added.
He likened the Japanese tax hikes to a 1937 U.S. tax increase, which pushed the economy back into recession and kept the depression from ending until World War II began.
Higher taxes could cause a recession in Japan and put further pressure on the yen, McGee added.
"The hard thing is going to be to keep (the dollar) from going up later."

A key factor supporting the dollar rally versus the yen is the U.S. economy's relative strength compared with the Japanese economy's continuing struggle after the collapse of its real estate and stock market 'bubbles' in the early 1990s.

Plagued with gaping budget deficits, the Japanese government plans to tighten fiscal policy on April 1 but has been reluctant to introduce a supplemental budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year to help fuel economic growth.

"We're very interested in seeing how well the Japanese economy performs in the second quarter (of the calendar year)," said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Securities Inc. "That's going to be the key for the dollar-yen exchange rate."
Growth will be weak in the April-June period, Widness said. "But, I don't think it's enough to derail the expansion."
In January, Shimpei Nukaya, vice minister of the Economic Planning Agency (EPA), told reporters the economy might slow in the April-June quarter after the consumption tax is raised on April 1.

But Nukaya said the supplementary budget for the 1996/97 fiscal year would ease, to some extent, the pain of the fiscal tightening. The planning agency estimated that Japan's economy will grow around 1.9 percent in fiscal 1997/98 after an estimated 2.5 percent growth in the current fiscal year.

The dollar sank to a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995. Since then, the greenback has staged a spectacular recovery, soaring some 56 percent to 124.82 yen on February 14. On Tuesday morning, it traded near 122 yen.
Currency markets are abuzz with speculation about whether the dollar rally will continue.
A statement issued after the latest meeting of financial leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) major industrial nations indicated the strong dollar gains should end.
Amid fear that the Bank of Japan might intervene to stem any further dollar rise, the U.S currency has failed to break above the crucial 125-yen barrier.

"I think the dollar strengthened from the 115 level to above 120 on the expectations that the Japanese economy was going to weaken in reaction to the tax hikes," Widness said. "So, I think the market has already discounted that."
In short, Widness contended the dollar is near its peak.
That view is shared by James Burtle, director of foreign exchange service at the WEFA Group. Burtle said he expects the dollar to trade around 113 yen at the end of the year.
